c1.story:
Cement is the most boring product in India, and one of the most interesting businesses. A grey powder sold in heavy paper bags. Little brand loyalty beyond a familiar logo at the dealer's counter. No technology anyone outside the industry would recognise. And yet cement has been the stage for one of the most dramatic corporate battles of the decade.

In 2022 Gautam Adani's group bought Holcim's stakes in Ambuja Cements and ACC, and announced that it meant to challenge UltraTech, the Aditya Birla group's cement company, for the top spot. What followed was an arms race. Both groups announced huge capacity additions, and both went shopping. Adani bought Sanghi, Penna and Orient; UltraTech bought control of India Cements. Within a couple of years the two groups held about half the country's capacity.

That battle explains the three doors. The pan-India majors, UltraTech, Ambuja, ACC, Shree Cement and Dalmia Bharat, have plants in every region, national brands and the lowest cost per tonne. In most regions they decide whether there is a price war. Their bet is consolidation: the bigger they get, the better prices should behave.

The regional players, Ramco in the south, Star Cement in the northeast, JK Lakshmi, Birla Corporation and Mangalam in the north and centre, own one or two limestone clusters and a strong local brand. They take whatever price the regional market allows, which usually means whatever the majors allow. For many of them, the most likely ending is a takeover.

Every regional cement stock has two prices: what its plants earn, and what a major might pay for them.

The third door sells something extra. JK Cement makes white cement and wall putty, which earn more than grey cement. JSW Cement and Nuvoco lean on slag, a by-product of steelmaking, to make blended cement more cheaply. Each still runs a grey cement business that behaves like everyone else's, so the niche cushions the cycle rather than escaping it.
c1.read:
Three tiles, one per door. Read each top to bottom.

  • The name and line under it tell you the company's position: plants in every region and the power to set prices, one or two clusters and a price taker, or a niche product alongside grey cement.
  • The tickers are listed companies behind each door; click one for its stock page. The first tile has the most names, and two of them, AMBUJACEM and ACC, belong to the same group.
  • The profit bar is the key element. The majors sit at medium, not high: even the biggest cement company sells a commodity whose price swings with fuel and competition. The regionals sit at low, because they take the price the majors set and buy fuel in smaller lots. The value-added specialists sit at medium, the niche lifting them above the regionals.
  • The last line is the bet. The regional blurb mentions being bought out; the major blurb mentions the big two buying the rest. They are two sides of the same trade.

Notice that no door gets a high bar. That is the single most important fact about cement as an investment: it is a cyclical commodity business, and even the leaders keep only a middling share of what they earn across the cycle.

Below the tiles, the analogy maps the doors onto a national dairy, a local one and a paneer maker, and the so-what line gives the twist: the gap between a major and a regional narrows each time a major buys a regional. Consolidation is slowly redrawing this card.

c2.story:
To understand cement, follow a lump of limestone on its journey to a building site.

It starts in a quarry next to the plant. Cement plants are built on top of limestone, not near cities, because limestone is the bulk of the raw material and is too heavy and cheap to haul far. The quarry is held on a lease auctioned by the state government, and that lease is the plant's licence to exist. Limestone sits in a few belts: Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Andhra and Telangana, Gujarat and Karnataka. So that is where the kilns are.

The second station is fuel and power, and this is where the money goes. A kiln must be heated to well over a thousand degrees to turn limestone into clinker, and it burns petcoke, a refinery by-product, or coal, much of it imported from the US Gulf, Indonesia and Australia. That is why this kitchen has a foreign band: the industry's biggest cost is set in dollars, in markets India does not control. Plants have spent heavily on waste-heat recovery, which turns hot exhaust into electricity, and on solar, to shrink that bill.

Station three is the kiln itself, where limestone becomes clinker, the hard grey nodule that is cement's active ingredient. Station four grinds the clinker with gypsum, and often with fly ash from power plants or slag from steel plants, into the powder that goes into bags. Increasingly this happens at a grinding unit near the city rather than at the mine, because it is cheaper to ship clinker in bulk and grind it close to the customer.

Station five is the dealer and the site. Most bags go through retail dealers to individual home builders; bulk goes to developers, contractors and ready-mix plants.

Cement is a national industry made of dozens of local markets, each a few hundred kilometres wide.

The reason is freight. Fuel and freight each cost as much as the raw material itself, so cement rarely travels more than a few hundred kilometres. The price in Hyderabad and the price in Delhi are set by different plants and can move in opposite directions in the same quarter.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the band row underneath.

The five boxes follow the limestone from quarry to building site: mines, fuel and power, clinker kilns, grinding and blending, dealers and sites. Under each name you see what happens and who stands there. The kiln box names the limestone belts; the grinding box names who leans on slag and who on white cement.

The band row is the interesting part. The first band, captive leases, is coloured as Indian: every listed company holds its own limestone. The second band is marked as the rival: imported petcoke. That is the one station the industry does not control. The third and fourth bands, kilns and grinding, are Indian listed. The fifth, dealers and builders, is grey: customers and channels, not producers.

So the picture is of an industry that owns its raw material and its factories but buys its single largest cost from abroad, at world prices, in dollars. That is why a spike in petcoke or Indonesian coal hits every company at once, a couple of quarters later as inventory rolls over.

The note under the bands tells you where the plants cluster and why freight matters so much. The so-what line gives the punchline: cement is a local market dressed up as a national industry.

Use the diagram to place news. A petcoke price move lands on station two and reaches margins in about two quarters. A state limestone auction is a station one story that decides where a new plant can go. A new grinding unit near a city is a station four move to cut freight. A housing slowdown starts at station five and travels back up the chain.

c3.story:
Who buys cement? The easy answer is builders, and that sends many investors in the wrong direction. They picture highways and metros, read the budget's infrastructure numbers, and buy cement stocks. Then the quarter disappoints.

The real answer is that roughly two-thirds of cement goes into housing, and the biggest single slice of that is not big developers but families building their own homes. A farmer in Uttar Pradesh adding a floor after a good harvest. A shopkeeper in a Telangana town replacing a tin roof with a concrete one. A family in a Pune suburb finally building on a plot they bought years ago. They buy bags from a local dealer, a few at a time, and their decisions move with rural incomes, the monsoon, housing subsidy schemes and the bag price itself.

India's biggest cement customer is not a contractor. It is a family adding a floor after a good harvest.

Urban real estate is the next slice: apartment towers and offices, buying in bulk and increasingly as ready-mix concrete delivered by truck. That follows home sales, launches, interest rates and developer cash.

Then government. Roads, railways, metros, ports, canals and government housing all buy cement, and they move with budgets, award pace and the election calendar. A strong infrastructure budget helps, but it is a minority of demand. Government work also tends to stall before elections, as it did in 2024, and pick up afterwards.

Industrial and warehousing demand, factories, data centres, logistics parks, is the newest slice, and it follows private capex.

This mix matters for timing. A good monsoon lifts rural income, and that money becomes home building in the dry season after the harvest. Infrastructure spending is lumpier and tends to follow budget releases. Urban housing follows developer launches by about a quarter. So a cement company's year is really three overlapping calendars: the farmer's, the finance ministry's and the developer's.
c3.read:
Seven tiles, one per customer group. Read each in three lines: who buys, what they buy and what moves them.

  • Individual home builders come first, described as the largest single slice. They buy bags through dealers, and they move with rural income and the monsoon. This tile alone can make or break a quarter.
  • Urban real estate buys bulk and ready-mix, moving with home sales and rates.
  • Roads and highways, railways, metros and ports, and irrigation and water are the government's tiles, moved by budgets, award cycles and, in irrigation's case, monsoon failures that trigger spending.
  • Industrial and warehousing follows private capex.
  • Government housing follows scheme targets and fund releases before elections.

A useful way to read the grid is by what the customer buys. Bags go to the home builder and government housing; bulk goes to everyone else. Bags sold through dealers usually fetch a better price than bulk sold to contractors, so a company selling more through dealers tends to earn more per tonne, while one leaning on infrastructure contracts trades margin for volume.

Then read the so-what line, which carries the key fact: roughly two-thirds of cement goes into housing. So a strong infrastructure budget cannot rescue a quarter when the home builder stays away, but a good monsoon and a rural recovery can. If you read only one tile, read the first.

c4.story:
Here is the oddity at the heart of cement economics: the raw material is almost free, and the cost is everything you do to it afterwards.

Limestone sits in the company's own quarry, next to the plant. It costs little to dig. But to turn it into cement you have to heat it in a kiln to well over a thousand degrees, which burns a great deal of petcoke or coal, and run giant mills to grind it, which burns a great deal of electricity. Then you have to move a heavy, low-value powder to customers by truck and rail. Fuel and freight together eat a large part of each rupee of sales.

In cement, the clay is free. You pay for the fire and the truck.

That is why the industry is judged on one number: EBITDA per tonne, the operating profit on each tonne sold. It strips out size and lets you compare a giant with a regional. And it swings wildly. In the best years it can be double what it is in the worst, because it is a thin slice squeezed between two big numbers: the bag price on top and the fuel and freight bill underneath.

Think about the arithmetic. A few rupees more per bag, across millions of tonnes, is the whole year's profit swing. A spike in petcoke, as in 2022 after the war in Ukraine, can eat half the margin within a couple of quarters. And the two can move together the wrong way: in 2024 the majors cut prices to win share, and EBITDA per tonne fell to multi-year lows even though fuel had eased.

The other line worth watching is capex. A new integrated plant costs a lot per tonne of capacity and takes about three years to build. When the whole industry adds capacity faster than demand grows, as it is doing now, utilisation stays low and every company is tempted to cut price to fill its new kilns. Depreciation rises before the volumes arrive.

What barely matters? Working capital. Dealers pay fast and inventory is low; cement is a cash business, which is one reason the majors can fund their acquisition sprees.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for a pan-India major and for a regional player. Read each left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar here is power and fuel, the kiln's appetite. It takes about a quarter of sales for the major and a little more for the regional, which buys in smaller lots and has less waste-heat and solar power of its own.
  • The opex bar is freight, raw material and people, and it is the biggest bite: about half of sales for the major, a little more for the regional. Freight is a large part of it, which is why plant location matters so much.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is the cost of the plants and the loans that built them, slightly higher for the regional.
  • The last bar is what is left. The major keeps about a sixth of each rupee. The regional keeps roughly half that.

Notice how small the gap is on each individual bar, and how big it becomes at the end. A few rupees more on fuel, freight and interest, each one modest, together halve the profit. That is scale economics in one picture, and it is why regionals keep selling themselves to majors. These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the amount.

Below the charts, the list marks what matters. EBITDA per tonne, realisation per tonne, power and fuel per tonne, freight per tonne, and capex and asset turn all get a yes. Depreciation and interest get a sometimes. Working capital gets a no. The habit to build: read EBITDA per tonne first, then split it into price, fuel and freight.

c5.story:
The cement cycle runs on two clocks at once. One is demand: housing and government capex. The other is margin: the gap between the bag price and the cost of fuel. And beneath both ticks a third, slower clock: capacity, which decides how long any good spell lasts.

The last cycle shows all three. In 2020 and 2021, after the lockdown emptied plants for a quarter, demand came back strongly with rural housing, and companies emerged with leaner costs. Prices were firm, fuel was cheap, and EBITDA per tonne hit records. Stocks rerated. At the peak in 2021, company after company announced new capacity, and the Adani group set out to enter by buying Ambuja and ACC.

Then the margin clock broke. In 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, petcoke and imported coal prices roughly doubled. Cement companies could not raise prices fast enough, and margins collapsed. Fuel eased in 2023, but by then the capacity clock had started: UltraTech and Adani both announced plans to become far larger. In 2024 that turned into a price war. The majors chased volume, bag prices fell to their lowest in five years, and the general election stalled government work. Meanwhile the consolidation wave swept through the regionals.

A fuel shock breaks margins for a year. A capacity race can break them for a cycle.

The bottom came across 2024 and 2025. Fuel stayed cheap, prices recovered from the spring of 2025, and in September the GST Council cut the tax on cement from twenty-eight to eighteen percent, lowering the bag price for home builders. JSW Cement listed. Demand turned up in the second half.

Today the arrow sits in early up-cycle. Volumes are growing, prices are holding and fuel is cheap. But the capacity clock is still running fast, and that is the clock that decides how far this up-cycle goes.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The last cycle's years label them: boom in 2020 and 2021, peak in 2021, bust from 2022 to 2024 and bottom from 2024 into 2025. The arrow points at early up-cycle, just past the bottom, with the detail line that prices are firm, fuel is cheap and capacity is racing. That last phrase is the caveat built into the label itself. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

Notice that the bust was long and had two causes: a fuel shock in 2022 and a price war in 2024. The timeline shows them as two separate bust years with a neutral year between.

The timeline runs from 2019: neutral, then boom in 2020 and 2021, bust in 2022, neutral in 2023, bust again in 2024, neutral in 2025 and the latest entry marked as now.

The four hands are what move the arrow.

  • Bag prices, region by region: firm but uneven, up. Watch the south and east for proof the price war is over, and the north for signs it is not.
  • Petcoke and imported coal price: low, marked up because low fuel helps.
  • Industry capacity utilisation: around seventy percent, flat. Above three-quarters gives producers pricing power; below two-thirds invites a price war.
  • Volume growth versus capacity growth: demand catching up, mixed.

Two hands up, one flat, one mixed. Price and fuel are helping now; utilisation and the capacity race decide whether it lasts.

c6.story:
If you could know only two things about the cement industry each month, you would ask for the bag price in each region and the price of petcoke. Between them, they tell you EBITDA per tonne before any company reports it.

Start with demand. Housing is roughly two-thirds of cement sales, so it carries the heaviest weight. Government capital spending, on roads, railways, metros and irrigation, carries the same weight in this table, because it lifts bulk volumes in every region at once and because it is the swing factor a budget can change. Together they decide how many tonnes are sold.

Then the cost dials. Petcoke and imported coal are the largest cost line and are bought largely in dollars, so they carry three dots, with a lag: fuel bought today burns a couple of quarters later. Diesel is the freight line, because trucks move most cement. And a weaker rupee raises the fuel bill further.

Housing sets the tonnes. Petcoke sets the margin. The bag price sets the mood.

Interest rates work slowly: they slow housing starts a few quarters after a hike. The monsoon is two-faced. During the rains sites shut and the September quarter is always weak. After a good monsoon, rural incomes rise and home building picks up in the dry season. So the same rainfall hurts one quarter and helps the next two.

Then the confirming dials. The official cement production index and the infrastructure goods output index give a monthly read on volumes before companies report. And the election calendar: government work slows before polls and labour goes home to vote, so an election quarter tends to be a lost quarter for cement, as 2024 showed.

Notice what is missing from this list: any dial for cement prices themselves. That is because the bag price is not an outside force. It is the industry's own verdict on all the other dials, and on how hard the majors want to compete.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the business. Notice that the channels split cleanly into volume (housing, government spending, interest rates, monsoon, elections, the two output indices) and cost (petcoke, diesel, the rupee).
  • A rise does: a green up arrow helps, a red down arrow hurts, a diamond cuts both ways. The red rows are mostly costs, petcoke and coal, diesel and the dollar, plus interest rates and the election calendar. The one diamond is the monsoon, which shuts sites during the rains and lifts rural building after.
  • Weight: three dots on three rows: housing demand, government capital spending and the petcoke and coal price. Two demand dials and one cost dial.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: the realty index as a proxy for housing, the infrastructure index for government spending, a coal output series for fuel, Brent crude for diesel, the money-market rate, the rupee, the cement production index and infrastructure goods output. The monsoon and the election calendar show a dash; for those, read the weather office and the poll schedule.

Read the three-dot rows first. Then note the so-what line's twist: it picks regional bag prices and petcoke as the two to track, and bag prices are not a row in this table at all. That is because the bag price is the industry's own output, the result of these dials and of competition, which is why it appears on the lead indicators chart instead.

c7.story:
Cement's bottlenecks fall into two groups: the one that decides returns for years, and the many that make individual quarters noisy.

The big one is capacity outrunning demand. The two largest groups are racing each other to add plants and grinding units, and the regionals they have bought come with expansion plans of their own. Each new plant is rational for its owner: in a consolidating industry, scale means lower costs and more say over prices. But together they keep national utilisation around seventy percent. At that level every company has idle kilns and a reason to cut price to fill them. That is the structural bottleneck, and the so-what line says it will decide returns.

Each new plant makes sense alone. Together they cap the price.

Freight is the second structural constraint. Cement cannot travel far profitably, so a plant in a region with too much capacity is stuck with that region's price. Rail wagons run short in the busy season. This is why location, not just size, separates good plants from bad ones.

Fuel is cyclical: petcoke and imported coal follow crude and global freight, and a spike takes a couple of quarters to work through inventory and cannot always be passed on.

Then the recurring headlines. The Competition Commission has fined the industry heavily before for price coordination, in a case that ran for years, and it watches price rises and clears every acquisition. The monsoon quarter is always weak, and investors who forget that misread a seasonal dip as a downturn almost every year. Elections pause government payments and project awards.

The slow ones are limestone and carbon. New limestone leases are auctioned by states, with delays, royalties and local disputes, and an old plant running out of limestone nearby is a real risk. And cement is one of the most carbon-heavy industries in the world. India's carbon credit scheme and Europe's border tax are starting to put a price on clinker, which will favour blended cement and green power over time.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck: its name, why it bites and a severity label. There are eight rows, and the labels sort them into four kinds.

  • Structural: capacity outrunning demand, and freight and lead distance. Permanent features of the next few years. They belong in your valuation and in the multiple you will pay.
  • Cyclical: fuel price swings, which follow crude and global freight.
  • Recurring: three rows, cartel scrutiny, the monsoon quarter and the election lull. These are the headlines and seasonal dips that move a stock for a quarter without changing its value.
  • Slow: limestone leases and carbon. They work over years, quietly reshaping where plants can go and which kind of cement earns the best return.

The so-what line gives the reading order: the capacity race decides returns for the next few years, and the rest are quarter-level noise that creates entry points if you can tell them apart.

That second half is the practical use of this table. When a cement stock falls on a weak September quarter, check whether it is the monsoon row. When it falls before an election, check the election row. When it falls because a major announced another round of plants in its region, that is the structural row, and it deserves far more weight. The skill this card teaches is telling recurring noise from structural news.

c8.story:
Cement looks like a free market, but the rulebook decides where a plant can go, what goes into the bag and how far prices can rise together.

Start at the beginning: limestone. Since 2015 new mineral leases have been auctioned by state governments rather than handed out, and the winning bids, royalties and district mineral fund contributions all add to cost. A company without a lease near demand cannot build a plant there, however much it wants to. The environment ministry, the central pollution board and state boards then clear mines and plants and set dust and emission limits. A delayed clearance is a delayed plant; a closure order is a lost quarter.

The Competition Commission is the rule every cement investor should keep in mind. In a long-running case it found major producers guilty of coordinating prices and fined them heavily. Today it clears every acquisition in the consolidation wave and keeps an eye on synchronised price rises. Its presence is one reason the big two cannot simply raise prices together whenever they like.

In cement, the competition regulator is a quiet participant in every price rise.

The Bureau of Indian Standards sets how much fly ash and slag can go into each grade of cement. That sounds technical, but blending is the cheapest way to cut both cost and carbon, so the standards decide how far companies can push it.

The newest rule is the GST cut. In September 2025 the GST Council moved cement from twenty-eight to eighteen percent, lowering the bag price for home builders. It was a one-time lift to demand and a test of pass-through: did companies cut prices by the full amount, or keep some?

And the carbon rules are coming. India's carbon credit trading scheme sets emission intensity targets for cement plants, rewarding blended cement and green power. Europe's carbon border tax barely touches Indian cement today, because India exports little, but it is the template other markets may copy.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who, what, why you care, and status.

  • Always: four rows, the mines ministry and states on limestone leases, the environment ministry and pollution boards, the Competition Commission and the Bureau of Indian Standards. These are the permanent architecture of the business: where plants can go, how they must run, how prices may move and what goes into the bag.
  • New: the GST Council's cut from twenty-eight to eighteen percent. The one fresh demand tailwind on the page.
  • Live: the Bureau of Energy Efficiency's perform-achieve-trade scheme and Indian Railways freight policy. One pushes efficiency; the other can add a busy-season surcharge to the freight bill.
  • Coming: India's carbon credit scheme and the EU carbon border tax. Both put a price on clinker, which favours blended cement and green power.

Read the coming rows with the third door from card one in mind. Companies that already blend heavily with slag or fly ash and run waste-heat and solar power stand to gain from carbon rules, while high-clinker plants will face a new cost.

Use the why-you-care column when a headline lands. An acquisition headline means a Competition Commission review. A limestone auction tells you where the next plant will go. A railway surcharge is a margin hit in the busy season. Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Five forces asks who keeps the money. In cement the answer is surprisingly clear, and it explains the consolidation wave.

Start with the one force that barely exists: substitutes. Nothing replaces cement in an Indian building. Steel structures and prefabricated panels nibble at the edges, but a house, a bridge or a metro viaduct needs concrete, and concrete needs cement. That is why both shapes are tiny on that spoke.

Now rivalry, where the two doors differ most. In most regions, two groups decide whether there will be a price war. If one of them decides to chase volume, as happened in 2024, prices fall and everyone suffers. But the majors chose it, and they can afford it. A regional player has no such choice. It lives with whatever the majors decide, which is why its rivalry score is at the maximum.

Suppliers squeeze everyone, because petcoke and coal are bought at world prices. The majors soften it by buying in bulk and running their own waste-heat and solar power; regionals have less of both.

Buyers split in two. Millions of individual home builders have no power at all over the bag price. But infrastructure contractors and ready-mix plants buying in bulk negotiate hard, and in a weak market they get their discount.

And entrants? A new integrated plant needs a limestone lease, environmental clearance and about three years. So the real entry route is acquisition, and only the majors can afford it. That is the force that has reshaped the industry since 2022: majors entering new regions by buying the regionals already there.

In cement, you do not enter a region. You buy your way in.

The result is the so-what line: the majors keep the most profit, and the regionals increasingly trade on takeover value as much as on earnings.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: pan-India majors and regional players. Look at size first. The regional shape is larger on four spokes and level on the fifth. It never dips inside the major's shape.

  • Rivalry: three for regionals, the maximum, against two for majors. The majors start the price war; the regionals suffer it.
  • Suppliers: two and a half against two. Both face world fuel prices, regionals slightly worse.
  • Buyers: two against one and a half. Bulk buyers push regionals harder.
  • Entrants: two against one, as wide a gap as rivalry. For a major, entry is mostly a threat it controls by acquiring. For a regional, a major arriving in its cluster is the entrant.
  • Substitutes: half a point for both, the smallest score on the chart. Nothing replaces cement.

Notice the shape of the major: low on substitutes and entrants, higher on rivalry and suppliers. Its pressures come from inside the industry and from fuel, not from outsiders.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a reason. Redraw it for the company you own. A regional in a tight market with no new capacity nearby deserves a lower rivalry score. A major with a high share of green power deserves a lower supplier score. A regional already acquired and folded into a major's network has, in effect, moved to the other shape.

c10.story:
A cement results call can drown you in plant names, commissioning timelines and region-by-region commentary. Eight numbers cut through it, and the first one does most of the work.

EBITDA per tonne is the sector's one number: operating profit on each tonne sold. It lets you compare a giant with a regional, and this quarter with the worst quarter of the last bust. But on its own it hides the cause, so split it. Realisation per tonne is the achieved price after discounts; a fall while volumes rise is the signature of a price war. Power and fuel cost per tonne is the fuel cycle plus the company's green-power progress. Freight cost per tonne and lead distance tell you whether the plants are in the right places. A margin rise built on cheap petcoke is borrowed from the fuel market and will be repaid; one built on realisation is earned.

Split EBITDA per tonne into price, fuel and freight. Only one of the three is truly earned.

Then the volume and capacity numbers. Volume growth tells you whether demand is real and whether the company is taking share: growing faster than the industry, especially after a new plant comes on, is the sign of a good location. Capacity utilisation is the industry's temperature: above three-quarters, producers have pricing power; below two-thirds, someone will cut price.

Finally, the expansion numbers, the ones that matter most in a capacity race. Net debt to EBITDA tells you whether an acquisition spree is affordable or whether the acquirer overpaid. Capex to depreciation tells you how hard the company is racing. Racing is fine if utilisation is high; racing while utilisation falls is how the next price war gets funded.

Read them in that order, the margin split first, then volume and utilisation, then the balance sheet, and the commentary on the call starts to sound like confirmation rather than news.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number: what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, the only column with figures. Notice that several benchmarks come in pairs, one for majors and a lower one for regionals, or a level paired with a direction, such as rising quarter on quarter.
  • Today's industry median is filled in for the five rows that map to annual filings: EBITDA per tonne, read through the EBITDA margin; volume growth, read through sales growth; power and fuel, read as a share of sales; net debt to EBITDA; and capex to depreciation. Realisation, utilisation and freight come from company presentations and industry data, so they show a dash.

A caution: the median for the first row is a margin as a share of sales, not rupees per tonne, because filings report the first and not the second. Use it to see where the typical company sits in the cycle, and use the company's own per-tonne figure from its presentation for the benchmark comparison.

The trick is to read three things together for each company: its own number, the median and the good mark. In an early up-cycle with a capacity overhang, the company to prefer shows rising EBITDA per tonne driven by realisation rather than fuel, utilisation above the industry, and capex to depreciation that is high but matched by rising volumes. The capex row is the one to watch most closely this cycle.

c11.story:
Cement is one of the most forecastable industries on this site, if you know where to look. Almost everything that decides a quarter is visible weeks or months before the company reports.

Start at the same quarter. Brokers and analysts run dealer price checks city by city every few weeks, and those checks are realisation per tonne in real time. The government's cement production index and railway cement loading give industry volume before results. Read together, they are the quarter's top line.

One quarter ahead: home registrations and developer launches, because apartments sold today pour concrete next quarter, and the release of central and state capex funds, because money released to contractors becomes bulk orders.

Two quarters ahead sit three dots, and they are the most valuable. Petcoke and Indonesian coal prices: fuel bought today burns in the kiln two quarters later, so a spike today is a margin hit two results away. Monsoon rainfall and kharif sowing: rural cash after the harvest becomes home building in the dry season. And announced capacity commissioning dates: a new plant arriving in your company's region is price pressure ahead.

Furthest out, three quarters, is the highway award pace: roads awarded today buy cement about a year out.

In cement, the fuel you buy today is the margin you report two quarters later.

Put the signals together and you get the three-sign rule: bag prices rising, fuel flat or falling, demand outgrowing capacity. Today two of the three are ticking. Prices are firm though uneven by region, and petcoke is low, though crude is a risk. The missing sign is demand outgrowing capacity, because capacity is still racing. That is an early recovery with an overhang, and it is why the call prefers the low-cost majors and the regionals with new plants in tight regions, and warns against paying for takeover hopes alone.

The chart places each signal along a line by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read its channel.

For cement the dots spread across the whole line. Two sit at the same quarter: dealer price checks, and the cement production index with rail loading. Two sit one quarter ahead: home registrations and launches, and capex releases. Three sit two quarters ahead: petcoke and coal prices, monsoon and kharif sowing, and announced capacity commissioning. One sits on the far right at three quarters: the highway award pace.

Use the chart as a reading order, right to left. The highway awards tell you about bulk demand a year out. The two-quarter cluster tells you about margin through fuel, rural volume through the monsoon and price pressure through new capacity: the three things that decide EBITDA per tonne two results from now. The one-quarter dots tell you about next quarter's volume. The left-hand dots confirm this quarter.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. Ticks on bag prices rising, noted as firm but uneven by region, and fuel flat or falling, noted as petcoke low with crude a risk. A cross on demand outgrowing capacity, noted as capacity still racing. Two of three, which the rule calls early recovery.

The call box gives the view, the points behind it, and what would change it: a petcoke and coal spike on the back of crude, a fresh price war led by one of the majors, or a housing slowdown from higher rates or a weak monsoon. Those are your alerts. The first lines up with the two-quarter fuel dot: if crude spikes, you have roughly two quarters before it shows in results.
